L52: # 守護吉澳的門神
L53: 
L54: 吉澳西澳有一座天后宮，在整個島較高的位置，守護村民。訪問中發現村民對於島上天后像的由來有不同說法，有些說是相傳一尊天后娘娘的神像在吉澳對開海面飄浮，附近居民發現後，就把它帶回陸上供奉，而這個說法亦得到古物諮詢委員會採用，作為對吉澳天后宮歷史建築物的簡要。另一說法則是，荔枝窩村民認為天后娘娘神像是屬於荔枝窩的，曾經一度嘗試登島取回，但在卜杯求問天后娘娘意願後，天后娘娘屬意留在吉澳，故一直由吉澳島上村民供奉。
L55: 
L56: 根據古物諮詢委員會的報告，吉澳天后宮於 1880 年(光緒六年)前建成，拜祭天后娘娘的善信多為客家人及漁民，以祈求風調雨順，大吉大利，每逢天后誕、元宵節與十年一度的安龍打醮等節日，村民都會齊集天后宮慶祝，1957 年前曾騰出部份地方作為學校。[1] 即使現時島上居民漸少，但每年的天后誕仍是備受重視的節日。[2]
L57: 
L58: 整座天后宮設計精細，有不少石灣陶瓷裝飾、木雕等，而最為人注目的應該是正門的門神。乍看或者覺得現時的門神跟其他廟宇的門神沒有明顯分別，但這對門神其實是在2006年重新裝上，原本的一對門神則存放於吉澳故事館內。
L59: 最早記載的門神是神荼、鬱壘，古人認為桃木可辟邪，而立桃板於家門，驅除不祥，及後演變成於桃木板畫上神荼、鬱壘二神，或書寫二神的名字，稱為「桃符」，其作用類似今天的門神。[3] 現時本地最具代表及最常見的將軍門神，便是唐代名將秦叔寶與尉遲恭，典故一般認為是與兩位名將為皇帝唐太宗守夜門有關，亦成為民間家宅、廟宇等守衛大門的神靈，防範鬼魂入侵。[4]
L60: 
L61: 而這對在吉澳天后廟內的舊門神又有什麼特別呢? 訪問吉澳故事館黃館長，他稱之為「假門神」、「鬼佬門神」，顧名思議則是說門神的樣貌似西方人。據說殖民時代英軍登上吉澳，誤闖天后廟而毀壞大門，故後來為安撫村民，便由啹喀兵（英軍屬下的兵團）協助重繪一對門神，他們半靠記憶、半靠想像，再參考對方的臉重新畫上；亦有另一說法，門神是根據啤牌（撲克）上國王的造型加以發揮的，直至現時村民向外介紹都會提及這些掌故，並欣喜一對「真門神」重新裝上。筆者認為「鬼佬門神」的形象是參考了古代兵將形象又混合了其他元素，足蹬黑布靴子，頭上戴有色彩繽紛的帽，腰間戴有牛面的掛飾和銅錢(村民有說似卡通比卡超)，背面帶有「福」字的靠旗，充滿想像空間。
L62: 不論那個掌故更貼近事實，這對舊門神的確承載著村民在島上的記憶，亦一直守護村民十分重視的天后宮。而且由漁農自然護理署推出的吉澳文化徑的官方論述中的天后廟，亦以一對舊門神作介紹。
L63: 
L64: 香港可見的門神主要呈現方式包括門畫、浮雕、石膏雕塑、紙或木版印刷等，以往選用的門神物料更是一種身份象徵，現時在港懂得繪畫或雕刻門神的師傅已寥寥可數。而現時在吉澳天后廟木門上是一對浮雕門神，在香港已非常少見，顏色鮮艷，更配有金彩點綴，氣勢非凡，據村民所說是在內地訂製的，手工十分仔細，木材優質。門上左邊(左右門神以神明或祖先神位面向而定)是秦叔寶，其形象為粉面、鳳眼，身穿金武甲、手持刀、掛弓，足蹬雲頭靴，背有飄帶；右邊的尉遲恭則面黑、怒目，身穿金武甲，手持斧、掛箭，足蹬雲頭靴，背有飄帶，未有如一般的門神，佩帶有四支靠旗。[5] 兩者雙眼是對望的，以示兩方合作對付鬼怪，如果安裝錯了，就真是「貼錯門神」了。
L65: 島上不少民居、家祠、廟宇依然貼有或裝上門神，反映了島上居民仍然保留這個信仰或習俗，鎮宅僻邪。而其中一對版畫門神，筆者找了大半年，這對門神竟然在島上無處不在，顏色依然鮮艷，與村民了解後才得知，他們每年農曆新年都會到上水街市附近攤檔購買，與新年每家每戶換上新的揮春的習俗一樣，都是一種吉祥的象徵，祈求家宅平安。
L66: 
L67: 下次大家再次到訪吉澳，不坊多留意島上門神的不同造型與製作方式，一探村內的習俗。

L50: # A Map of Deities in Sha Tau Kok (Part I)
L51: 
L52: In everyday life in Hong Kong, people often encounter temples of all sizes—ranging from large Tin Hau temples spanning several shopfronts to small household shrines tucked inside shops. To understand this phenomenon, it is useful to explore the different functions temples served in rural communities.
L53: 
L54: Part 1 – Faith
L55: Temples and deities represent different social and regional groups. In Sha Tau Kok, for example, there are currently two Tin Hau temples. One is primarily used by waterborne communities, while the other is associated with Hakka villagers. Although both temples honor the same deity, Tin Hau, they symbolize different groups within the community.
L56: 
L57: Part 2 – Defining Village Boundaries
L58: Most temples in the Sha Tau Kok area are either Kwan Tai temples or Tin Hau temples. The Hakka migrated to Hong Kong around the Great Clearance in 1669, and they felt their social status was lower compared to the Cantonese. Building Kwan Tai and Tin Hau temples was a way to elevate their standing and voice. Compared to Kwan Tai and Tin Hau, the Earth God Pak Kung held a lower rank, yet he was the most frequently worshipped deity.
L59: Small Pak Kung temples were often found at the entrance and exit of villages, serving to mark the village boundaries.
L60: Part 3 – Festivals
L61: 
L62: Beyond Kwan Tai’s birthday (the 24th day of the sixth lunar month) and Tin Hau’s birthday (the 23rd day of the third lunar month), the Hing Chun Yeuk, the Nam Luk Yeuk, Yim Liu Ha Tin Hau Temple and Kat O Tin Hau Temple still preserve the tradition of holding “Tai Ping Ching Chiu” festival once every ten years.
L63: In the past, villagers often interpreted the forces of nature through the lens of feng shui and deities. It was traditionally believed that communities inevitably committed sins and became polluted in the course of living. Religious rituals such as communal purification ceremonies (Da Chiu) were therefore needed to restore purity to the human world.

L1@P0: Historic Building Appraisal
L2@P0: Tin Hau Temple
L3@P0: Sai O, Kat O, N.T.
L4@P0:  The Tin Hau Temple (天后宮) is situated in Sai O (西澳) on the western shore
L5@P0: of Kat O (吉澳, Crooked Island). It was built by villagers of Kat O, Hakkas and
L6@P0: Tankas (蜑家), who were mainly fishermen worshipping Tin Hau as their patron
L7@P0: deity. Kat O was once a major fishing market in Hong Kong which price of fish
L8@P0: and dried shrimp had dominant indication. The temple was built probably in 1763
L9@P0: as the temple bell has the dating inscribed on it. The temple is managed by a Tin
L10@P0: Hau Kung Rural Committee (天后宮值理會) which is also responsible for the Tin
L11@P0: Hau Festival (天后誕) activities and the management of the Kat O market in the
L12@P0: past. Part of the temple was used as school premises before 1930 until the Japanese
L13@P0: Occupation. After the war it continued to be the Kat O School until 1957 when the
L14@P0: school moved to a new premises.
L15@P0: Historical
L16@P0: Interest
L17@P0:  The sea-facing temple has a three-hall block in the middle with one annex
L18@P0: block connected to its left and right separated by two lanes. The temple is in Qing
L19@P0: vernacular style having pitched roofs supported by a system of timber brackets.
L20@P0: The original external greenbrick walls have been covered with cement dressing or
L21@P0: plastered. The granite steps at the recessed entrance however have been retained.
L22@P0: The most valuable relics of the temple are the Shiwan (石灣) ceramics made by its
L23@P0: Qiaoruzhang (巧如璋) kiln installed on its main ridge and on the gable friezes.
L24@P0: The former includes a pearl, two aoyus (鰲魚) and Chinese opera figures and the
L25@P0: latter mainly opera figurines. Other decorations such as the mouldings and facia
L26@P0: boards of the temple are also well preserved.
L27@P0: Architectural
L28@P0: Merit
L29@P0:  The temple is one of the Tin Hau type rare to witness over 200 years of
L30@P0: history in the north-eastern part of Hong Kong.
L31@P0: Rarity
L32@P0:  The well preserved temple with some minor alterations and additions has high
L33@P0: built heritage value.
L34@P0:  A number of repairs and renovations have been held without record. Some of
L35@P0: the unsympathetic changes can be reversed to the original.
L36@P0: Built
L37@P0: Heritage
L38@P0: Value
L39@P0: Authenticity
L40@P0:  Tin Hau Festival on the 23rd day of the third lunar month will be highly
L41@P0: celebrated at the temple and fa pow (花炮) competition is the highlight of the
L42@P0: festival. Da chius are also held every ten year on the ninth month of years ending
L43@P0: 6, that is, in 1976, 1986, 1996 and so on. The chiu is called On Lung Da Chiu (安
L44@P0: Social Value,
L45@P0: & Local
L46@P0: Interest

L48@P1: 龍打醮) normally held in front of the temple. Another chiu, called Ya Chiu (壓醮)
L49@P1: is also held between the normal chius. The deity of the temple is also invited to
L50@P1: attend the chiu festival of Tap Mun (塔門) nearby.
L51@P1: Number 974
